# Rasayel Bet the Company on _WhatsApp Closing B2B Deals_

Founded by a bootstrapper in a south Ireland fishing town, Rasayel turns WhatsApp into a sales channel that syncs with HubSpot - and it did it without raising a dollar.

Advertisement

By **YesPress Newsroom**Aug 7, 20267 min read

![Illustration of WhatsApp chat bubbles flowing into a CRM sales pipeline](https://yespress.io/img/profile-photos/rasayel-whatsapp-b2b-sales-yespress.svg)The Rasayel thesis in one picture: conversations that start in a chat thread end up as tracked deals inside the CRM. Illustration: YesPress Newsroom.

Open the WhatsApp of any working salesperson and you will find a graveyard of half-closed deals. A pricing question here, a "let me check with my team" there, a voice note from a buyer who went quiet three weeks ago. None of it is in the CRM. Most of it is on a personal phone that walks out the door the day that rep quits. Rasayel is a company built on the belief that this mess is not a support problem to be ticketed away - it is the actual sales floor, and nobody had bothered to instrument it.

That is the whole bet. Rasayel is a WhatsApp platform aimed squarely at B2B sales teams, and it made a decision most of its rivals refused to make: to be useful to a smaller group of people and ignore everyone else. WATI courts small teams doing light support. [Respond.io](https://respond.io/) chases high-volume, omnichannel B2C. Tidio leans into webchat and e-commerce. Rasayel looked at that crowded shelf and picked the one seat nobody was sitting in.

"Track every conversation, automate follow ups, and sync WhatsApp with your CRM - so your team sells faster, stays organized, and never drops a deal."
— Rasayel's own product pitch

## // The unglamorous insight

The insight underneath Rasayel is almost boring, which is usually a sign it is right. Buyers moved to WhatsApp years ago. In large parts of Europe, the Middle East, Latin America and Asia, asking a customer to "reply to my email" is asking them to do something they simply will not do. Sales already happens in the chat thread. The CRM, the system of record that was supposed to capture every customer touch, went quietly blind the moment the conversation left email and phone.

Rasayel's answer is a shared team inbox that sits on top of the official WhatsApp Business API, plus a native two-way bridge into the CRM. A message a rep sends from Rasayel shows up on the HubSpot contact record. A reply from the buyer becomes an activity attached to the deal. Nothing lives on a personal phone. Nothing walks out the door.

Around that spine sit the things a sales team actually needs day to day: assignment rules so leads do not sit unanswered, private notes so a manager can coach mid-deal, sales sequences for the follow-ups everyone means to send and never does, WhatsApp Forms to qualify a lead without a call, and an AI chatbot to catch inbound at 2 a.m. The company pitches a 30-minute setup and free migration, which tells you who it is really courting - teams that have been burned by month-long onboarding somewhere else.

## // What "for sales" actually changes

It is easy to wave at "we're built for sales" as marketing. In Rasayel's case it changes the product's shape. A support tool optimizes for closing tickets fast. A sales tool optimizes for moving a specific human buyer one step closer to yes, over days or weeks, often across several people on both sides. Those are different physics. The CRM sync is not a nice-to-have bolted on at the end - it is the reason the whole thing exists, because in B2B the deal record is the source of truth, not the chat.

Bars show breadth of intended use case, drawn from each product's own positioning. Not a feature ranking - the point is that these tools are aimed at different buyers.

That focus is also a discipline. Every feature request from an e-commerce marketer or a bulk-broadcast spammer is a request Rasayel can decline without guilt, because it is not the customer. Knowing what you are not is an underrated superpower in software, and it is most of why a small company can hold its own against rivals with far bigger war chests.

## // The money story is the strategy

Here is the number that makes people lean in: public company profiles list Rasayel at roughly $3.1M in annual recurring revenue with $0 in disclosed outside funding. In a category where competitors raised tens of millions, that is not a footnote. It is the strategy showing up on the balance sheet. No funding means no pressure to chase every adjacent market to justify a valuation, which is exactly the pressure that would have blurred the "just B2B sales" focus.

The founder's history rhymes with this. Tarek Khalil, Rasayel's CEO, is a repeat bootstrapper. Before this he co-founded Octopods in 2019 - a tool that plugged live-chat systems into other messaging channels - and grew it toward roughly $1M ARR without the venture treadmill. Before that he was a product engineer at Intercom, a company that arguably taught a generation what business messaging could be. Rasayel is his second turn at the same essential problem: getting conversations into the systems that run a business.

The company describes itself as "five years in the making." In a world of six-month rocket ships, patience is the contrarian move.

## // A company with no building

The team behind Rasayel is stranger and more interesting than the polished website suggests. Khalil runs the company from a small fishing town in rural south Ireland. His co-founder and COO, Mohamed Elbadwihi, works out of Alberta, Canada. The rest of the roughly 28-person team is scattered across Portugal, Belgium, Egypt and North Macedonia. There is no headquarters in any meaningful sense. Remote is not a perk they tolerated after the pandemic - it is the operating system the company was assembled on, complete with a published manifesto on how to make a distributed culture actually work.

There is something fitting about a company that sells "meet your customers where they are" being built by people who never share a room. The medium is the message. If your buyers are on WhatsApp and your engineers are in six time zones, then asynchronous, written, well-organized communication is not a nicety - it is the only thing that keeps the whole arrangement from falling apart. That is arguably the same product Rasayel sells to its customers.

## // The buyer nobody was serving

To understand why the focus works, picture the specific person Rasayel is built for. A sales manager at a mid-sized software company, running a team of ten reps across three countries. Half their pipeline lives in WhatsApp because that is where the buyers reply. The manager cannot see any of it. They cannot tell which deals have gone cold, which reps are ghosting leads, or what was actually promised on a call that happened in a voice note. When a rep resigns, the relationships leave with them. This person does not want another omnichannel dashboard or a cleverer chatbot. They want the conversations their team is already having to become visible, coachable and owned by the company.

That is a narrow buyer, and it is exactly why the incumbents missed them. A tool built for e-commerce broadcasts optimizes for blasting a promotion to 50,000 contacts. A tool built for support optimizes for deflection and first-response time. Neither is designed around a slow, high-stakes, multi-touch B2B deal where the whole game is context. Rasayel's sales sequences, private notes and CRM sync are all answers to that one manager's daily frustration. When you can name your customer that precisely, the roadmap writes itself.

## // The honest risks

None of this is a guarantee. Rasayel is a business built almost entirely on top of a platform it does not own. Meta sets the rules of the WhatsApp Business API, changes pricing on its own schedule, and could in theory build shared inboxes and CRM sync itself. Betting your company on a single channel controlled by a trillion-dollar gatekeeper is a real risk, and no amount of founder discipline erases it. The bull case is that Meta has shown no appetite for building deep, vertical sales software, and that the CRM integrations and workflow are the moat, not the WhatsApp connection itself.

The other risk is the mirror image of the strength. A narrow focus is a great way to win a small market and a bad way to become enormous. Rasayel has chosen to be excellent at one thing for one buyer rather than adequate at many. Whether that ceiling is high enough to matter is the open question - but at ~$3.1M ARR with no investors to answer to, it is a question the company gets to answer on its own timeline. Most startups never earn that luxury.

What is easy to steal from Rasayel, whatever happens next, is the shape of the idea: find the place your customers already live, notice that your industry's systems of record have gone blind to it, and build the bridge. It is not a flashy pitch. It is just a real one.

## // Questions people ask

What does Rasayel do?

It is a WhatsApp platform for B2B sales teams: a shared team inbox, automation, AI chatbots and sales sequences, plus two-way sync with CRMs like HubSpot, Pipedrive and Salesforce so conversations become tracked deals instead of getting lost on personal phones.

How is it different from WATI, respond.io and Tidio?

WATI targets small teams and light support, respond.io targets high-volume omnichannel B2C, and Tidio leans into webchat and e-commerce support. Rasayel focuses narrowly on B2B sales teams closing deals on WhatsApp, with deep CRM sync as the core.

Does Rasayel integrate with HubSpot?

Yes - native two-way integration with HubSpot, plus Pipedrive, Zapier and a developer API. WhatsApp messages appear on the CRM record and reps can message from inside it.

Who founded Rasayel and when?

Co-founded in February 2022 by Tarek Khalil (CEO, formerly a product engineer at Intercom and founder of Octopods) and Mohamed Elbadwihi (COO).

Is Rasayel venture-funded?

Public profiles list no disclosed outside funding. The company reportedly reached around $3.1M ARR as a bootstrapped, fully remote business.
